opus-5.5.text:
I think a truly representative work isn't defined by how many citations it gets, or even by whether it beats the state of the art on some benchmark at the time. For me, it comes down to a few things.

First, it should change how people *think* about a problem, not just how well they solve it. A lot of papers improve numbers by a point or two, and that's valuable, but the works that really last are the ones where afterwards people say, "Oh, of course, that's how we should have been looking at it all along." It reframes the question.

Second, it should be simple. I've always been drawn to ideas that you can explain in a sentence or two. If a method needs ten tricks stacked together to work, it's usually not capturing something fundamental. Simplicity is often a sign that you've found something true about the problem, and it's also what lets other people pick it up, build on it, and carry it somewhere you didn't expect.

Third, it should survive time. The field moves incredibly fast. Architectures come and go, and what's hot this year may look naive in two years. So a representative work is one whose core insight still holds after the specific implementation becomes outdated. Sometimes the model itself gets replaced, but the principle behind it keeps showing up in new systems.

And maybe the last thing is a bit more personal: it should reflect the researcher's own taste and conviction. Many of the works I respect most were not following the trend at the time. Sometimes they were going against the consensus, revisiting something people thought was settled, or asking a question that seemed unfashionable. I think having the courage to do that, and then doing it rigorously, is what makes a work feel like it truly represents someone, rather than just representing the moment.

So in short: it changes how people think, it's simple enough to spread, it holds up over time, and it carries a clear point of view.

r001.rationale: The candidate says representative work changes how people think and reframes a problem, but does not say it causes an abrupt shift in the field’s research trajectory.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, partly because the field moves so fast that "representative" can mean very different things depending on when you ask.

For me, a truly representative work isn't the one with the most citations or the biggest benchmark number at the time. It's the one that changes how people think about a problem, so that a few years later the idea feels obvious, almost like it was always there. ResNet is the classic example. The skip connection is embarrassingly simple when you see it, but it reshaped how everyone designs deep networks, and nobody can imagine not having it now.

I'd say there are a few ingredients. First, the idea has to be simple enough to be transferable. If a method only works with twenty tricks stacked on top of each other, it won't travel. Second, it should reveal something true about the problem rather than just exploit a quirk of a dataset. When we did ConvNeXt, the point wasn't really "ConvNets beat Transformers." The point was to ask honestly which design choices actually matter, and to show that a lot of the perceived gap came from training recipes and architecture details rather than from attention itself. That kind of clarity is what makes work last.

And third, honestly, a representative work needs a bit of luck in timing. The same idea proposed too early gets ignored because the compute or data isn't there. Too late and it's incremental. You can't fully control that, so I tell students not to chase the "representative work" directly. Chase the question you genuinely find confusing, try to answer it as cleanly as possible, and if the answer is real, the community will eventually recognize it.

One more thing I'd add: I'm increasingly skeptical of defining representativeness purely by leaderboard performance. In the era of scaling, a lot of impressive numbers come from resources rather than insight. The work I respect most is the kind where you can read the paper and come away understanding something you didn't before. That understanding compounds. Numbers get overtaken in six months.

r001.rationale: The response says representative work changes how people think and cites ResNet as reshaping network design, but it does not clearly say that such work causes an abrupt shift in the field’s research trajectory.

astra-6.text:
For me, a representative work is something that captures how you think about research. It’s not necessarily your most cited paper or the one with the best benchmark result. It’s a piece of work where you identified a meaningful question and offered a perspective that other people could build on.

In AI, results move so quickly that being number one at a particular moment doesn’t tell you very much about lasting value. I would ask: after the specific numbers become outdated, is there still an idea people find useful? Does the work change how they approach a problem, or make something complicated easier to understand?

There’s also a personal dimension. A representative work should reflect your taste—what you believe matters and what you choose to pursue. Sometimes you only recognize that work in retrospect, once you see which ideas keep influencing your own research and other people’s.

r001.rationale: The response says a representative work may change how people approach a problem and influence later research, but it does not say it causes an abrupt shift in the field’s research trajectory.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, a truly representative work is one that captures how you think about a problem. It’s not necessarily your most cited paper or the one with the best benchmark result. It’s the work where you can say: this question mattered to me, I had a particular intuition, and I followed it through.

In AI, results can become outdated very quickly. So I would ask: after the numbers are surpassed, is there still an idea that people find useful? Did the work change how they approach a problem, or help them ask a better question? If something survives beyond the particular model or benchmark, that’s what makes it representative to me.

r001.rationale: The response says representative work may change how people approach a problem or help them ask better questions, but it does not describe an abrupt shift in the field’s research trajectory.
